quote: The fairest action of our human life, / Is scorning to revenge an injury: / For who forgives without a further strife, / His adversary’s heart to him doth tie.
source: Elizabeth Cary, The Tragedy of Mariam, the close of Act 4, lines 1 to 4 (Chorus) (1613 quarto)
speaker: Chorus
note: Corrected: the spelling is modernised from the 1613 quarto, which prints humane, injurie and adversaries, but the pointing is the quarto’s, including the comma in line 1 and the colon in line 2. The modernised anthology text, which travels as Revenge of Injuries and often under the name Lady Carew, prints no comma and a semicolon.

evidence.where: Two independent transcriptions of the 1613 quarto, both read this run: the Malone Society Reprint scan at archive.org, item tragedyofmariam100caryrich, downloaded in full; and the Celebration of Women Writers transcription at digital.library.upenn.edu, whose title page reads London, printed by Thomas Creede for Richard Hawkins, 1613. The circulating modernised text was surveyed through Open Library full text search, which returns 261 printings of the line.
evidence.edition: The Tragedy of Mariam, the Fair Queen of Jewry, 1613 quarto, read in the Malone Society Reprint edited by A. C. Dunstan with W. W. Greg, 1914, and in the Upenn transcription; spelling modernised in the shipped line, pointing kept as the quarto points it
evidence.locator: the Chorus that closes Act 4, its first four lines. In the Malone reprint the speech heading stands at line 1903 and the quatrain at lines 1904 to 1907, fixed by the reprint’s own textual note, which records the turned n of fcorniug at line 1905, the second line of the quatrain. The reprint’s marginal 1900 stands beside This curse of thine shall be return’d on thee, 1910 beside If we a worthy enemie doe finde, and 1940 beside Actus quintus, Scoena prima, which is the scene that follows this Chorus.

reason: The refutation is right on every count I could test, and none of it touches the attribution, which holds: the quatrain opens the Chorus that closes Act 4, immediately before Actus quintus, and the poem is Cary’s, not the ghost Lady Carew of the anthologies. What was wrong was the card. The quarto points line 1 with a comma after life, which the earlier verdict dropped while keeping the quarto’s colon in line 2, so the shipped string was a hybrid of two texts and existed in neither; the comma is restored. The earlier note claimed the colon stands in modern editions alike, and that is false: of the modernised printings I surveyed, the common anthology text prints no comma and a semicolon, one reader prints a comma and a semicolon, and only an outlier schoolbook prints the colon. The note now says plainly that the pointing is the quarto’s and that the anthology text differs. The Malone line number in the evidence was also off by one and is corrected to 1904 to 1907, confirmed by the reprint’s own note at 1905. Finally the source line put a bare date between the locator and the speaker, against rule 5 and against this file’s settled practice of speaker first and imprint last, and it said chorus twice in one line; it now reads locator, speaker, edition. shipped.js: not shipped, nothing near, Elizabeth Cary at 0 of 3, not banned, and she is a woman, which the month’s floor wants. In scope, 1613, drama, publishable with no warning, and on theme, since the stanza argues that declining revenge is the braver conquest.
